nodes.label: InsForge
nodes.rationale: All-in-one, open-source Postgres-based backend (BaaS) that gives the app a database, authentication, file storage, edge functions, realtime, an AI model gateway, and payments through one platform, so the project doesn't have to integrate each of those separately.

nodes.label: insforge skill
nodes.rationale: App code with the @insforge/sdk client: database CRUD, auth, storage, edge functions, realtime, AI, email, and Stripe payments.

nodes.label: insforge-cli skill
nodes.rationale: Backend and infrastructure via the insforge CLI: projects, SQL, migrations, RLS policies, storage buckets, functions, secrets, payment setup, schedules, deploys.

nodes.label: insforge-debug skill
nodes.rationale: Diagnosing failures (SDK/HTTP errors, RLS denials, auth and OAuth issues) and running security or performance audits.

nodes.label: insforge-integrations skill
nodes.rationale: Wiring external auth providers (Clerk, Auth0, WorkOS, Better Auth, etc.) for JWT-based RLS, or the OKX x402 payment facilitator.

nodes.label: find-skills skill
nodes.rationale: Discovering additional skills on demand.

nodes.label: .env.local credentials
nodes.rationale: App code reads InsForge keys from .env.local; keys must never be hardcoded or committed.

nodes.label: .insforge/project.json credentials
nodes.rationale: The insforge CLI reads project credentials from .insforge/project.json rather than .env.local.

nodes.label: Database inserts take an array
nodes.rationale: insert([{ ... }]) — the InsForge SDK's insert call takes an array even for a single row.

nodes.label: Reference users via auth.users(id) / auth.uid()
nodes.rationale: Standard InsForge pattern: reference users with auth.users(id) in schema and use auth.uid() inside RLS policies to key visibility to the authenticated caller.

nodes.label: Storage upload persists url and key
nodes.rationale: For storage uploads, both the returned url and key must be persisted so the object is addressable both publicly and via the storage API.
nodes.norm_label: storage upload persists url and key

nodes.label: Witness
nodes.rationale: Renamed from Ghost Work. A witness testifies, and a claim without corroboration isn't testimony, it's rumor — the name encodes the confirm-against-a-second-source mechanic that is the project's core mechanism.

nodes.label: Ghost Work
nodes.rationale: Original project name before the rename to Witness.

nodes.label: The pivot: make the database the detector
nodes.rationale: In the original architecture the source-degradation claim (restricting to one connector produces a confident, wrong performance review) is unverifiable — a judge has to take on faith that no hidden code branch like a source-name conditional faked it. Moving attribution into Postgres temporal joins and gating every read through views keyed on run.enabled_sources makes degradation a structural property of the schema instead of a promise of discipline, so the demo cannot cheat even if it wanted to. InsForge ends up holding the two things the project cannot fake: what counts as proof, and who is allowed to see it.
nodes.norm_label: the pivot: make the database the detector

nodes.label: confirm_attributions(run_id)
nodes.rationale: Postgres function implementing Stage 5 rules (a) and (b) as temporal SQL joins (e.g. joining ticket_state where the assignee differs from the message author and the ticket closed within the confirmation window after the message) — turns attribution into a temporal join rather than an LLM judgment call, and is the core of the demo running inside InsForge.

nodes.label: Source-scoped views (degradation guarantee)
nodes.rationale: visible_source_event, visible_ticket_state, etc. are each filtered by the run's enabled_sources so disabling a source empties the table from the query's point of view — the 'must degrade for real, not fake the output' requirement is satisfied by construction rather than by code discipline.

nodes.label: Classification cache
nodes.rationale: Keyed on sha256(body) so classification is source-independent; without it the live toggle demo would require re-classifying hundreds of messages on stage with Pipeshift latency deciding whether the demo passes. Makes the second run return in under a second, which is what makes the live re-run demo physically possible.

nodes.label: RLS + Auth
nodes.rationale: Own-data / manager-of-reports visibility enforced via auth.uid() and a SECURITY DEFINER team-membership helper, so the ethics answer to 'isn't this dangerous' is a database guarantee rather than a promise about the UI.

nodes.label: Storage — run snapshots
nodes.rationale: Raw HydraDB pull per run dumped to a bucket so runs replay deterministically from snapshot; covers the brief's 'cache one successful full run as demo fallback' and insures against venue wifi failure.

nodes.label: pgvector fuzzy reference resolution
nodes.rationale: Embeds messages and ticket titles and cosine-matches them so references like 'the auth timeout thing' resolve to a ticket even without a regex-matchable ID — meaningfully raises recall since most real Slack unblocks don't cite a ticket ID.

nodes.label: Realtime — live run stream
nodes.rationale: run_stage_event insert triggers realtime.publish to a channel so pipeline stages fire live on screen. The brief lists 'no dashboard' as a non-goal for time-budget reasons, not design reasons; framed as the most watchable thing buildable for the cost.

nodes.label: Schedules (nightly run)
nodes.rationale: Nightly scheduled run against the RocketRide endpoint, cheap coverage worth the minutes.

nodes.label: Secrets management
nodes.rationale: HydraDB / Pipeshift keys referenced from edge functions — correct practice regardless of the demo.

nodes.label: Edge function (report endpoint)
nodes.rationale: Public read-only report endpoint so the report is fetchable without RocketRide being awake.

nodes.label: Branch workflow
nodes.rationale: Apply the risky RLS migration on a backend branch first, merge when green.

nodes.label: identity_claim table
nodes.rationale: Entity resolution is never clean; keeps the claims and their evidence, not just the winning merge.

nodes.label: source_event table
nodes.rationale: Normalized landing table for everything HydraDB returns.

nodes.label: ticket_state table
nodes.rationale: The second source that makes confirmation possible.

nodes.label: classification table
nodes.rationale: Keyed by content_hash, not by message, so classifications survive re-runs.

nodes.label: run_stage_event table
nodes.rationale: Realtime source for live per-run stage progress.

nodes.label: confirm_window_hours run parameter
nodes.rationale: Lives on the run, not in code. The brief's 48h/24h are guesses that may yield zero confirmations on small data; widening the window live without a redeploy is the difference between a demo and an apology.

nodes.label: reference.method field
nodes.rationale: Records whether a citation came from regex or vector match, so when the tool claims an artifact is evidence it can say how it found it.

nodes.label: Divergence formula bug (low-visible people)
nodes.rationale: invisible / (visible + invisible) breaks on low-visible people — a new hire with two Slack messages and zero PRs scores 1.0 and tops the ranking. Fix: require a minimum of 2 confirmed attributions before a person is rankable.

nodes.label: Stage 6 contradicts the pitch
nodes.rationale: The project promises 'the result isn't a score' but Stage 6 ranks by a computed score. Fix: keep divergence as an internal sort key and never render the number, since a rendered score risks being screenshotted into a real performance review.

nodes.label: Gmail source (contributes nothing)
nodes.rationale: Expected to contribute nothing but kept in the toggle array because four toggleable sources makes the degradation demo richer; no logic gets built for it, and the team says so plainly if asked.

nodes.label: Risk zero
nodes.rationale: The demo requires at least one Slack message referencing a ticket assigned to someone else that closed inside the window. If that pair doesn't exist in the synced HydraDB data, checking must happen first thing in the morning, while widening the window or seeding a fixture is still cheap.

nodes.label: Fallback: drop Pipeshift entirely
nodes.rationale: If behind schedule, fall back to regex-only reference extraction with rules (a) and (b) unchanged; the attribution engine and degradation guarantee both survive because they never depended on the LLM classification step.

nodes.label: Maria unblocked Chen on ENG-412 (example finding)
nodes.rationale: Illustrative confirmed finding used to demonstrate both the confirmation mechanism (Slack message references ENG-412, assigned to Chen, closed 2h14m later) and the degradation break (same endpoint restricted to Slack only shows Maria with zero confirmed contributions).
nodes.norm_label: maria unblocked chen on eng-412 (example finding)

nodes.label: Thesis: restrict to one connector -> confident wrong review
nodes.rationale: The original brief's central claim, used as the opening blockquote of 'The spark': scoping the tool to one connector doesn't make the answer go blank, it produces a confident, wrong performance review. Repeated on stage as 'your engineering dashboard is lying to you.'
nodes.norm_label: thesis: restrict to one connector -> confident wrong review

nodes.label: Problem statement (PRD §1)
nodes.rationale: Managers evaluate engineers on system-of-record credit (commits, PRs, tickets closed), so high-leverage but uncredited work — unblocking a teammate, catching a bug in review, triaging an incident — is invisible to every dashboard and invisible at review time.

nodes.label: MVP thesis: degradation must be provable
nodes.rationale: Restricting the tool to one connector must make the output become a confident, wrong performance review rather than going blank, and the MVP must make that provable, not merely observable — the falsifiability bar the whole build is designed around.
nodes.norm_label: mvp thesis: degradation must be provable

nodes.label: Users & visibility (PRD §3)
nodes.rationale: Engineer sees own ghost work, manager sees direct reports only, nobody sees the whole org — ranking everyone is the failure mode, not the feature; enforced by RLS, not by UI.

nodes.label: P0 scope — ships or no demo
nodes.norm_label: p0 scope — ships or no demo

nodes.label: P1 scope — ships if on schedule
nodes.norm_label: p1 scope — ships if on schedule

nodes.label: P2 scope — nice, cut without regret
nodes.norm_label: p2 scope — nice, cut without regret

nodes.label: Explicit non-goals
nodes.rationale: No dashboard, no auth/UI polish, no fine-tuning, no score presented as objective truth, no write-back to source systems, no historical trending, no multi-org tenancy.

nodes.label: Success criteria (PRD §5)
nodes.rationale: Five pass/fail criteria; criteria 3 (Slack-only run yields 0 confirmed findings, no redeploy) and 4 (the view definition itself shows the enabled_sources gate) together are described as the actual submission — everything else is support.

nodes.label: HydraDB
nodes.rationale: Owns cross-source identity resolution and raw event/ticket pulls from Slack/GitHub/Linear; confirmation is impossible without knowing that a Slack handle and a Linear assignee are the same or different people, and nothing else in the stack can produce that resolution.

nodes.label: Pipeshift
nodes.rationale: Classifies messages (unblock/review/triage/decision/noise) with strict JSON output, turning 'this message mentions ENG-412' into 'this message unblocked someone on ENG-412'; rule (a) confirms the link, Pipeshift characterizes the help.

nodes.label: RocketRide
nodes.rationale: Owns the public endpoint, stage orchestration, bounded-concurrency LLM fan-out with per-message retry on malformed JSON, and checkpoint/resume so a crashed run resumes rather than restarts — its role was deliberately restored after moving attribution logic into Postgres thinned it.

nodes.label: InsForge's role in the architecture
nodes.rationale: Owns the attribution engine, degradation guarantee, classification cache, access control, and snapshots — 'the detector itself,' and also what makes the live re-run physically possible during a demo.

nodes.label: POST /run request contract
nodes.rationale: sources is the toggle; changing it requires no deploy. replay_snapshot reruns from a cached HydraDB pull for offline determinism.

nodes.label: degraded response block
nodes.rationale: Declares which attribution rules could not run and why, framed explicitly as a product feature rather than debug output — a tool that reports what it cannot see is the opposite of the dashboards being criticized.

nodes.label: Access control (PRD §8)
nodes.rationale: RLS is on for person, attribution, and source_event; an engineer sees rows where person_id matches the current auth.uid()'s person, a manager sees direct reports via a SECURITY DEFINER helper chosen to avoid RLS recursion, and no policy grants org-wide read — that absence is the point.

nodes.label: public.reports_to(uuid)
nodes.rationale: SECURITY DEFINER helper used to determine manager-of-reports visibility without RLS recursion.

nodes.label: Degradation mechanism (PRD §8, SQL example)
nodes.rationale: Every read in the attribution path goes through a view like visible_ticket_state (security_invoker = true) gated on the run's enabled_sources; confirm_attributions() joins only against the visible_* views, never the base tables, so there is no code path that could produce a confirmation once a source is disabled.

nodes.label: Ranking formula (PRD §9)
nodes.rationale: visible = 1.0*prs + 1.0*tickets_closed + 0.3*commits; invisible = 1.0*confirmed_unblocks + 0.7*reviews + 0.5*triage; divergence = invisible / (visible + invisible).

nodes.label: Evidence floor
nodes.rationale: A person is not rankable below 2 confirmed attributions; without this correction a new hire with two Slack messages and zero PRs scores 1.0 divergence and tops the ranking, surfacing new hires and managers rather than ghost work.

nodes.label: Never render the divergence number
nodes.rationale: divergence is kept as an internal sort key only and never appears in the response, report, or on screen, because shipping a visible score contradicts the pitch's promise that the result isn't a score and risks being screenshotted into a real performance review.

nodes.label: Gmail source (PRD)
nodes.rationale: Expected to contribute nothing; stays in the sources array because four toggleable sources makes the degradation demo richer, but no logic gets built for it.

nodes.label: Problem statement (README)
nodes.rationale: Managers evaluate engineers on system-of-record credit; the highest-leverage work happens in Slack and gets credited to whoever closed the ticket afterward, invisible to every dashboard and invisible at review time.

nodes.label: How it works (README)
nodes.rationale: Attribution is framed as a temporal join rather than an LLM call, running entirely inside Postgres; every read in the attribution path goes through a view/function gated on enabled_sources so disabling a source removes rows structurally rather than via a skipped code branch. Access control follows the same structural pattern via RLS.

nodes.label: Migrations (README)
nodes.rationale: Migrations apply in filename order via the insforge CLI.
